findings.title: Raw proxy configuration saves silently replace newer edits
findings.confidence: Native service reproduction in a temporary directory
findings.trigger: Two operators read the same host nginx/Caddy file. A saves first; B later saves a valid edit made from the older buffer. The raw ConfigEditor is shared by the listed pages.
findings.expected: Refuse the stale save with a conflict and preserve B’s draft for review against A’s version.
findings.actual: GET /proxy/config returns content without an editor revision; PUT carries only kind/path/content/reload. WriteConfig serializes writes and validates syntax, but never compares the editor’s original bytes. In the temporary native probe both writes succeeded and B removed A’s change.
findings.impact: Valid syntax can still restore old upstreams, access policy or TLS settings. Serialization protects the staging procedure but does not prevent lost updates. The structured site builder has a separate digest guard; this finding concerns raw editing.
findings.recommendation: Return a content revision and require it on raw saves. Check under the existing writer lock before staging, return an explicit conflict and show the fresh file beside the retained draft.
findings.verification: The real proxysvc.ReadConfig/WriteConfig functions were exercised against private files. A private always-successful nginx stub replaced native validation; no host proxy, listener or reload was touched. The contract omission is also visible in the handler and frontend.

findings.title: Streamed database exports bypass session-expiry recovery
findings.confidence: Query-export browser reproduction; sibling paths source traced
findings.trigger: Let the browser session end after Query/Data has loaded, then export. The server returns 401 unauthorized.
findings.expected: Recognize the authentication failure, revalidate once and return to sign-in with the expiry explanation, just as ordinary feature requests do.
findings.actual: SQL result export, SQL table export and Mongo export call fetch directly and build their own ApiError without dispatching jd:authentication-lost. The query reproduction showed “Session expired”, remained at /databases/1/query and emitted zero auth-loss events and zero session rechecks.
findings.impact: The user remains inside a signed-in-looking workspace retrying a refused operation until a later ordinary API request or reload triggers recovery. Backend authentication still rejects the export; this is not an access bypass.
findings.recommendation: Share one authentication-response observer with streamed/binary response readers. Preserve streaming while centralizing recognized 401/account-disabled/password-change handling.
findings.verification: Confirmed against the fresh production frontend with an expired export response and expired session endpoint. Table/Mongo sibling readers were traced in source, not independently expired in the browser. Background polling can eventually recover the shell.

findings.title: A failed backup-job save can still replace its destination credentials
findings.trigger: Save a job with new storage credentials and changed metadata. The credential update succeeds, but the following metadata update fails or its request context is canceled.
findings.expected: Commit the credentials and definition together, or leave both old values when Save fails.
findings.actual: backups.Store.Update uses two independent UPDATE statements: first secrets_enc, then the job definition. There is no encompassing transaction. A private SQLite trigger that rejected the metadata write produced an error while the new credentials remained committed and the old job name remained.
findings.impact: A Save reported as failed can leave old bucket/endpoint settings paired with new keys. Scheduled backups may subsequently fail or use an unintended credential set.
findings.recommendation: Validate and seal first, then update credentials and metadata in one transaction or one statement. Add a meaningful regression that fails the metadata publication and verifies the credentials remain unchanged.
findings.verification: The actual backup Store.Update and Sealer ran against a newly created private SQLite database. A synthetic BEFORE UPDATE OF name failure modeled interruption of the second write. All key values were invented; no real destination was contacted.

evidence.note: Credential replacement commits before the definition write
Definition publication is a separate nontransactional statement
The API returns an error when the later statement fails

findings.title: Concurrent backup-job edits can quietly undo another editor’s choices
findings.confidence: Native lost-update mechanism reproduced; UI concurrency not separately exercised
findings.trigger: Two tabs read one backup job. A changes retention or included native dumps and saves; B saves another field from its older full-job draft.
findings.expected: Keep unrelated saved choices or surface a concurrent-edit conflict. A helper that adds a database dump should not replace a newer retention/schedule/source choice.
findings.actual: The form PUTs a full definition without an expected version. Store.Update rewrites every field with WHERE id only. In a temporary store, A’s retention of 10 was replaced with B’s stale value of 2 while both updates succeeded.
findings.impact: A job can silently lose retention, schedule, source, native-dump or recovery settings during overlapping edits. This is mapped as a behavior risk because the current job API does not promise versioned conflict handling.
findings.recommendation: Add a job revision and compare it on save, or use explicit field-level updates for narrow helpers with appropriate conflict handling.
findings.verification: Confirmed in the native store with two independent snapshots; no real backup ran. Source identifies the browser’s full-object PUT. Two concurrent browser dialogs were not independently exercised.

evidence.note: Job editor sends the complete definition
Metadata update compares only the record ID

known_limits.title: Archive coverage and checksums do not establish application recovery
known_limits.text: Coverage proves captured sources and verified artifact identity. A live database filesystem archive is not automatically transaction-consistent. Native database dumps and configured SQLite snapshots address their supported cases; the application checker proves only the supplied schema/canary check and is currently a single-container check.
known_limits.action: Use native dumps and an application-specific recovery drill; require evidence for the exact artifact where recovery matters.

known_limits.title: Required-factor recovery needs host access and account-scoped state
known_limits.text: Forgot-password guidance uses the host reset command; there is no email reset. Recovery codes are one-time display/consumption data. Hiding an enrollment panel does not erase the pending server seed. Tokens do not replace a browser session for personal factor management.
known_limits.action: Keep host access and safely retain recovery codes; judge enrollment/reset wording separately from backend enforcement.

known_limits.title: Stable labels exceed the evidence available for native integrations
known_limits.text: This audit built and tested the current code, but did not perform real package upgrades, native database restores, production deployment/certificate changes, host-account/SSH changes, dashboard reinstall/uninstall or real remote streams. Browser fixtures verify UI behavior and requests, not these operations’ success on the operator’s server.
known_limits.action: Before using a blanket stable claim, maintain a disposable native acceptance matrix for these integrations and their supported failure/recovery paths.
